<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 7 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Metric</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">7.3</span> The Levi-Civita Connection</h1></header>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>The geodesic equation (<a class="dg-xref" href="length-geodesics.html#eq_geodesic" data-kind="equation" data-label="eq_geodesic">7.1</a>) has the form of the autoparallel equation (<a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/parallel-transport-autoparallels.html#eq_autoparallel" data-kind="equation" data-label="eq_autoparallel">6.1</a>), with the connection coefficient functions replaced by the <strong>Christoffel symbols</strong> of <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> w.r.t. <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>,  <span class="math display" id="eq_christoffel_symbols">\begin{equation}
            \boxed{
                \big( \Gamma^{\text{LC}}_\mathscr{X} \big)^k_{ji} \coloneqq
                \frac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{km} \big( \partial_i g_{mj} + \partial_j g_{mi} - \partial_m g_{ij} \big) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}).
            } \tag{7.2}
        \end{equation}</span>  The <strong>Levi-Civita connection</strong> <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span> is the connection whose connection coefficient functions are, in every chart, the Christoffel symbols. With this choice, (<a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/parallel-transport-autoparallels.html#eq_autoparallel" data-kind="equation" data-label="eq_autoparallel">6.1</a>) becomes (<a class="dg-xref" href="length-geodesics.html#eq_geodesic" data-kind="equation" data-label="eq_geodesic">7.1</a>) term by term, so the <strong>straight</strong> curves of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span> are the <strong>extremal</strong> curves of the length. Moreover, exchanging <span class="math inline">\(i \leftrightarrow j\)</span> swaps the first two terms of the Christoffel symbols and leaves the third invariant (<span class="math inline">\(g_{ij} = g_{ji}\)</span>), so <span class="math inline">\((\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ji} = (\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ij}\)</span>, and <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span> is torsion free, <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}^k_{ji} = (\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ij} - (\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ji} = 0\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>A connection <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> is <strong>metric compatible</strong> if <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_\mathcal{X} g = 0\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\)</span>. In a chart,  <span class="math display" id="eq_metric_compatibility">\begin{equation}
            (\nabla_{\partial x_k} g)_{ij} = \partial_k g_{ij} - \Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} - \Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im} . \tag{7.3}
        \end{equation}</span>  As torsion freeness, metric compatibility of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span> follows from its definition: inserting the Christoffel symbols, <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} = \frac{1}{2} \big( \partial_k g_{ji} + \partial_i g_{jk} - \partial_j g_{ki} \big)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im} = \frac{1}{2} \big( \partial_k g_{ij} + \partial_j g_{ik} - \partial_i g_{kj} \big)\)</span>, whose sum is <span class="math inline">\(\partial_k g_{ij}\)</span>. Conversely, the two properties characterize it:</p>
<p><strong>Theorem (Levi-Civita).</strong> <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span> is the only torsion-free, metric-compatible connection on a metric manifold<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-7" id="fnref-7" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 7">7</a></sup>.</p></li>
<li><p>By metric compatibility, parallel transport with <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span> preserves <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span>: for vector fields <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_\gamma\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y}_\gamma\)</span> along <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\frac{d}{d\lambda} \, g(\mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma) = g(\nabla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma) + g(\mathcal{X}_\gamma, \nabla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{Y}_\gamma)\)</span> (Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="../proofs-and-additional-material/metric-properties.html#subsection_metric_prop_parallel" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_metric_prop_parallel">B.18.5</a>). Along an autoparallelly transported curve, <span class="math inline">\(g(v_\gamma, v_\gamma)\)</span>, and hence <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(s_\gamma\)</span>, are therefore constant. Its autoparallelly transported curves with <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \neq 0\)</span> are thus exactly the constant-speed geodesics, while those with <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma = 0\)</span>, not covered by the variational definition, are called <strong>null geodesics</strong>. For a general connection the two notions differ: autoparallels depend on <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span>, geodesics only on <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
<section class="dg-footnotes" role="doc-endnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-7" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-7" aria-label="Back to the text">7</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>See Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="../proofs-and-additional-material/proof-metric-compatibility.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_proof_metric_compatibility">B.17</a> for the proof, and for the fact that the Christoffel symbols of overlapping charts define the same connection.</p></div></div></section>
